To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CNA lesions attenuate stimulus-evoked cardiac responses in rats.
CNA lesions attenuate stimulus-evoked heart-rate changes that occur during acoustic startle tests.
CNA lesions attenuate stimulus-evoked cardiac decelerations, as well as stimulus-evoked freezing, and that stimulus-evoked freezing is attenuated more than stimulus-evoked decelerations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying the acquisition of fear.
the development of fear in response to acoustic stimuli and the role of the amygdala in this fear.
the neural systems that mediate the acquisition and expression of fear, and with the neural systems mediating the expression of fear in the absence of overt defensive behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CNA lesions attenuate stimulus-evoked heart-rate changes, but that the attenuation may reflect the development of conditioned fear.
the CNA lesions attenuated the development of fear as evidenced by the attenuation of stimulus-evoked heart changes.
amygdala lesions attenuate the development of conditioned fear during startle testing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amygdaloid central nucleus is a key component of a fear circuit that includes the acoustic startle circuit, and the circuitry for the development of fear.
the amygdaloid CNA is a critical component of a fear circuit that mediates fear responses to a broad range of stimuli.
fear conditioning during the startle procedure is mediated by the CNA and that the heart rate changes observed during this procedure can serve as a measure of the fear that is conditioned.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fear conditioning during acoustic startle is a useful paradigm for examining the role of the amygdala in the development of fear.
heart rate changes are a useful measure of fear in rats and that the CNA is involved in fear conditioning.
